title: Coronavirus (COVID-19) roundup, 24 to 28 August 2020
meta_description: Data and analysis related to the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic and its impact on our economy and society.
lede: Data and analysis related to the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic and its impact on our economy and society.

body.text: 28 August 2020

This page contains data and analysis published by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) from 24 to 28 August 2020. Go to our [live page](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/conditionsanddiseases/articles/coronaviruscovid19roundup/2020-03-26) for the most up-to-date insights on COVID-19.
28 August 2020

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by local area and socioeconomic deprivation
body.text: Deaths involving COVID-19 by local area and socioeconomic deprivation

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by local area and socioeconomic deprivation
body.text: We have published [provisional analysis of all deaths involving the coronavirus (COVID-19)](http://ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/birthsdeathsandmarriages/deaths/bulletins/deathsinvolvingcovid19bylocalareasanddeprivation/deathsoccurringbetween1marchand31july2020) that occurred in England and Wales between 1 March and 31 July 2020, (registered up to 15 August 2020), focusing on differences between local areas.

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by local area and socioeconomic deprivation
body.text: Our analysis shows that between March and July, there were 259,199 deaths occurring in England and Wales, 51,831 of which involved COVID-19 (20% of all deaths).

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by local area and socioeconomic deprivation
body.text: Over this period, there were 90.2 deaths involving COVID-19 per 100,000 people in England and Wales. Looking at both countries separately, this equates to 90.9 deaths per 100,000 people in England compared with 75.7 per 100,000 people in Wales.

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by local area and socioeconomic deprivation
body.text: Wales and all English regions recorded an increase in age-standardised mortality rates (ASMR) involving COVID-19 between March and April, followed by decreases in May through to July 2020. However, in England, for the month of July, the ASMR for deaths involving COVID-19 in the most deprived areas of the country was more than double that seen in the least deprived areas (3.1 deaths per 100,000 people compared with 1.4). This continued a theme seen in previous months.

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by local area and socioeconomic deprivation
body.text: Our analysis also shows that in July 2020, of the 336 local authority areas in England and Wales, 71 had no deaths in July involving COVID-19 and only two areas recorded more than 20 such deaths. These two areas were Leicester and Ashford, which saw 24 and 21 deaths involving COVID-19 respectively.

body.h2: International travel
body.text: International travel

body.h2: International travel
body.text: Restrictions on international travel have been in place since early 2020 because of the coronavirus (COVID-19). Recently, [the Foreign and Commonwealth Office (FCO) have started to ease travel restrictions for British travellers](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/coronavirus-covid-19-countries-and-territories-exempt-from-advice-against-all-but-essential-international-travel) where countries are assessed as “no longer presenting an unacceptably high risk to British people traveling abroad”. We have included analysis up to June 2020 of [recent international travel in our migration release.](http://ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/internationalmigration/bulletins/migrationstatisticsquarterlyreport/august2020#insights-into-recent-international-travel-patterns)

body.h2: International travel
body.text: These insights are not measures of international migration as they refer to travel patterns by all types of passengers, not just international migrants.

body.h2: International travel
body.h4: Home Office recent passenger arrivals
body.text: Home Office recent passenger arrivals

body.h2: International travel
body.h4: Home Office recent passenger arrivals
body.text: [Home Office statistics published today](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/immigration-statistics-year-ending-june-2020/how-many-people-come-to-the-uk-each-year-including-visitors) using Advanced Passenger Information (API) show that there were an estimated 1.3 million passenger arrivals (including returning UK residents) in April to June 2020. This is 97% (27.7 million) fewer than the same period in 2019, and it is because of the coronavirus travel restrictions.

body.h2: International travel

body.text: At the same time, the number of applications for visitor visas in Quarter 2 (Apr to June) 2020 was 99% lower than in the same period in 2019.

body.h2: International travel
body.h4: There has been widespread decline in international air travel to the UK since March 2020
body.text: There have been similar falls in the number of people travelling to and from the UK by sea. Provisional monthly figures produced by the Department for Transport, show the effect of travel restrictions on passenger numbers for short international ferry routes to Ireland and other European countries began to be seen in March 2020. Further impacts were then seen between April and June with the largest decrease in April 2020, when total passenger numbers dropped by 85% compared with the previous year.

body.h2: Number of working and workless households remains stable through lockdown
body.text: Number of working and workless households remains stable through lockdown

body.h2: Number of working and workless households remains stable through lockdown
body.text: [Between the start of April and the end of June 2020](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/employmentandemployeetypes/bulletins/workingandworklesshouseholds/apriltojune2020), there was an estimated 20.9 million households (where at least one member is aged 16 to 64 years) in the UK. Of these households, there were an estimated 12.5 million (59.6%) households that had an adult member in employment (working), while there were an estimated 2.7 million households (13.1%) where no member of the household was in employment (workless households). The number of households with a mix of at least one working and one workless adult was estimated at 5.7 million households (27.3%).

body.h2: Number of working and workless households remains stable through lockdown
body.text: The percentage of working households was unchanged compared with the same period a year ago, whereas the proportion of workless households has been falling since comparable records began. Over the past year, this has fallen by 0.6 percentage points from 13.7% of all households.

body.h2: Number of working and workless households remains stable through lockdown
body.text: The analysis was based on the Labour Force Survey and covered the period of implementation of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic lockdown and social distance measures. Thus, interviews relate to the period following the government closure of schools, the introduction of lockdown, and the announcement of measures aimed at protecting businesses and jobs.

body.h2: Crime in the UK dropped by almost one-third during the most restrictive period of the coronavirus (COVID-19) lockdown
body.text: The Crime Survey of England and Wales CSEW) estimated [a 32% decrease in total crime](http://ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/crimeandjustice/bulletins/coronavirusandcrimeinenglandandwales/august2020), excluding fraud and computer misuse, during April and May 2020, compared with a two-month average in the pre-lockdown period.

body.h2: Crime in the UK dropped by almost one-third during the most restrictive period of the coronavirus (COVID-19) lockdown
body.text: The drop was primarily the result of dramatic reductions in acquisitive offences, particularly domestic burglary and other theft of personal property.

body.h2: Crime in the UK dropped by almost one-third during the most restrictive period of the coronavirus (COVID-19) lockdown
body.text: The lockdown presented fewer opportunities for acquisitive crimes to take place, as people were increasingly at home and leisure and entertainment venues and shops were closed.

body.h2: Perceptions of unity have decreased as the pandemic has progressed
body.text: Perceptions of unity have decreased as the pandemic has progressed

body.h2: Perceptions of unity have decreased as the pandemic has progressed
body.text: As time has progressed through the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, [public perception on unity has altered](http://ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/wellbeing/bulletins/unityanddivisioningreatbritain/24aprilto28june2020). Between 24 April and 28 June 2020, the weekly Opinions and Lifestyle Survey (OPN) found that the percentage of adults who thought that Britain would be more united after the pandemic declined by 29 percentage points (from 57% in the first week of the period to 28% in the last week).

body.h2: Perceptions of unity have decreased as the pandemic has progressed
body.text: Over the period as a whole more people thought that Great Britain would be more united after the pandemic (46%) than before the outbreak (24%). When divided by nation, adults in Scotland were less likely (31%) to think Britain will be more united after the pandemic than those in England (47%) or Wales (44%).

body.h2: Perceptions of unity have decreased as the pandemic has progressed
body.h4: Although people in Scotland were more likely to think that Britain will be united after the coronavirus pandemic than to think it was united before, they were less likely to say this than those in England or Wales

body.text: A gender divide in perceptions of unity after the pandemic has emerged. While women were as likely as men to say that Britain was united before the pandemic, when asked to think about the future, 51% of women thought that the nations would be more united following the pandemic, while only 41% of men agreed.

Other factors that were associated with perceptions of unity included checking on neighbours, feeling like the community is available to support you, and thinking people are doing more to help others.

body.h2: Changing occupations
body.text: Changing occupations

body.h2: Changing occupations
body.text: We have analysed data from the Labour Force Survey (LFS) to work out how many workers have [changed occupations between January to March and April to June of 2020](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/employmentandemployeetypes/articles/coronavirusandoccupationalswitching/januarytojune2020).

body.h2: Changing occupations
body.text: This helps us understand the extent to which the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic has led to an increase in skills mismatch in the labour market (people doing jobs for which they are over- or under-qualified).

body.h2: Changing occupations
body.text: Our analysis suggests that the pandemic has so far had little impact on the number of people switching occupations. Around 1 in 16 employees (6.1%) changed occupation in the first half of 2020, compared with 5.7% in the same period last year.

body.h2: Changing occupations
body.text: This broadly reflects the impact of the government's job retention schemes, which encourage an attachment between individuals and a specific job.

body.h2: Changing occupations
body.text: Of those who changed occupation, more than half (52.5%) switched to a different industry. Again, this is little changed from the same period in 2019 (52.1%).
